summary: Specifies a way to check the source addresses of IPv6 packets using information learned through SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). It complements ingress filtering by controlling, at a finer level, which source addresses a given host or port may use.

eli5.summary: Imagine a mailroom that checks the return address on every letter against the person who actually dropped it off. This makes sure no one pretends to be somebody else on the same street.

questions: how does send help prevent address spoofing
how does savi prevent ipv6 source address spoofing
what are validating and trusted ports in savi
subtitle: How a switch uses SEND-secured Neighbor Discovery to pin each IPv6 source address to the port it legitimately belongs to.

tldr.problem: On a local IPv6 link, any host can try to send packets with someone else's source address, and ingress filtering alone does not control which addresses a given host or port may use.
tldr.mechanism: A SEND SAVI switch watches SEND-validated Neighbor Discovery messages and builds bindings between each IPv6 address and the switch port it was proven on. It then forwards data packets only if the source address matches the port, and it tests ownership with secured NUD probes when in doubt.
tldr.outcome: It works only on links where every host and router uses SEND, and it needs no changes to the hosts being checked. Ports must be configured correctly, since a wrongly configured port lets an attacker use any source address.

today: RFC 7219 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It applies only to links where all hosts and routers use SEND.

sections.title: What SEND SAVI Does
sections.content:
RFC 7219 specifies SEND SAVI, a way to validate the source addresses of IPv6 packets on a local link using the SEcure Neighbor Discovery protocol (SEND, RFC 3971). It complements ingress filtering (RFC 2827) by giving finer control over which source addresses are used.

The mechanism builds on messages that already exist: the Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) solicitation and advertisement from RFC 4862 and the Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD) solicitation and advertisement from RFC 4861. The document defines no new protocol and no new message, and it needs no changes in the nodes whose addresses are checked.

The scope is limited to links and prefixes where every IPv6 host and every IPv6 router uses SEND. For other networks the text points to alternatives such as FCFS SAVI (RFC 6620). The general framework is in RFC 7039.
sections.eli5: A school hall monitor only checks name tags that are really hard to fake. The monitor does not need the students to do anything new, and it only works if every student wears one of those tags.

sections.title: Bindings, Anchors and Local Traffic
sections.content:
A SEND SAVI device filters packets using bindings between a layer-2 binding anchor and an IPv6 address. Any SAVI solution is only as strong as its anchor, and a MAC address is easy to spoof, so implementations of this specification use switch ports as anchors.

SEND lets a node prove that it owns a Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) by signing Neighbor Discovery messages. SEND SAVI turns that proof into a binding between the CGA and the port from which packets with that source address are reasonable. Two events trigger binding creation:

  • A DAD solicitation, meaning a node is trying to configure an address.
  • Any other packet, including data, whose source address has no binding. The device then makes the sender prove ownership with a secured NUD solicitation, which must be answered with a secured NUD advertisement. Bindings are refreshed the same way.

The scope is the local link. Traffic from hosts using their own addresses is local traffic. Routers may forward packets with other source addresses, which is transit traffic. SEND SAVI validates local traffic and stops hosts from using off-link prefixes, but it cannot tell whether a router is allowed to forward a particular off-link address, so it recommends ingress filtering for that. Transit packets arriving on a Trusted port are forwarded without SAVI processing, and those arriving on a Validating port are discarded.
sections.eli5: The switch keeps a list saying which seat each person sits in. If a stranger says they are someone else, the switch sends a secret-handshake question to the real seat and only trusts the answer.

sections.title: Validating and Trusted Ports
sections.content:
To reduce work, SEND SAVI devices can form a protection perimeter, so packets are validated only where they enter the protected area, not at every device. Each port has a role. Validating ports do SEND SAVI filtering and binding creation. Trusted ports do limited processing: only SEND messages about certificates, prefix information and DAD are processed.

The port configuration guidelines are explicit:

  • Ports to other SEND SAVI devices MUST be Trusted.
  • Ports to routers MUST be Trusted. Routers then can send traffic with any source address, even those belonging to the link.
  • Ports to hosts SHOULD be Validating, otherwise the host can spoof source addresses.
  • No more than one host SHOULD be connected to each port, because sharing a port allows same-address packets and replay attacks.
  • Ports to a chain of legacy switches that have other SEND SAVI devices but no routers or hosts SHOULD be Trusted.

A SEND SAVI device MUST discard Router Advertisement messages received from Validating ports. It learns the link prefixes from the Prefix Information option (with the L bit set) of Router Advertisements arriving on Trusted ports, or from manual configuration. Special cases are covered too: multihomed hosts that share an address across interfaces are not directly supported, and routers attached dynamically, such as a phone acting as a router, are outside the default mechanism.
sections.eli5: Doors facing the grown-ups and other guards are marked trusted and wave people through. Doors facing visitors are marked checking, and everyone there gets inspected.

sections.title: Database, Prefix List and Constants
sections.content:
A device keeps a SEND SAVI Database populated from validated SEND messages. Each entry holds the IPv6 source address, the binding anchor (the port), a lifetime, a status (TENTATIVE_DAD, TENTATIVE_NUD, VALID, TESTING_VP or TESTING_VP'), an alternative binding anchor, and a creation time. The alternative anchor records a second port from which a DAD solicitation or data packet arrived while a different port was bound.

The SEND SAVI Prefix List has one entry per prefix with its lifetime. A device MUST send a Router Solicitation when it boots. It is also expected to be configured with a valid CGA address of its own, because it acts as a SEND node when it generates NUD solicitations. With VLAN support, the device behaves as if it ran one SEND SAVI process per customer VLAN.

Two constants control timing: TENT_LT is 500 milliseconds and DEFAULT_LT is 5 minutes.
sections.eli5: The switch keeps a notebook with each address, which seat it belongs to, and how long ago it checked. There are two timers: a quick one for short waits and a longer one for how long a note stays fresh.

sections.title: The Binding State Machine
sections.content:
Each source address has its own state machine in each device. NO_BIND means no binding exists, and it is the state for all addresses unless one is created. VALID, TENTATIVE_DAD, TESTING_VP and TESTING_VP' are forwarding states, where packets from the bound port are forwarded. NO_BIND and TENTATIVE_NUD are non-forwarding states.

The main paths work like this:

  • A validated DAD solicitation from a Validating port creates an entry in TENTATIVE_DAD with lifetime TENT_LT. A valid DAD advertisement from a Trusted port cancels it back to NO_BIND. If the lifetime expires, nobody else claimed the address, so it becomes VALID with lifetime DEFAULT_LT.
  • Any other packet from an unbound address triggers a secured NUD solicitation on that port and state TENTATIVE_NUD. A validated NUD advertisement makes the binding VALID, and a timeout returns to NO_BIND.
  • When a VALID binding expires, the device sends a secured NUD solicitation and enters TESTING_VP. Packets are still forwarded until the timer ends without an answer.
  • If a different Validating port shows up with a DAD solicitation for a bound address, the device probes the current port and enters TESTING_VP'. If the old port answers, the binding stays. If the timer expires, the alternative port becomes the anchor.

Only DAD solicitation, DAD advertisement, NUD advertisement and timer expiry move a binding between forwarding and non-forwarding states. Other packets never do. Advertisements are processed only as responses to solicitations. The device MUST join the solicited-node multicast group for every address not in NO_BIND, so it still sees DAD solicitations if the node moves.

The RFC's Figure 3 is explicitly a simplified version that does not show every transition.
sections.eli5: Each address is like a seat with a sign that says free, checking, or taken. The sign changes only when someone proves they belong or when the timer runs out.

sections.title: Walk-Through: Moves and Attacks
sections.content:
The RFC walks through two cases using two switches, SAVI1 and SAVI2. In the first, a host H with address IPH moves. If H moves to another port on the same switch and sends a DAD solicitation, SAVI1 enters TESTING_VP', probes the old port, hears nothing, and after TENT_LT binds the new port. If H moves to a different switch, SAVI2 goes to TENTATIVE_DAD and then VALID, while SAVI1 moves to NO_BIND after its own probe goes unanswered.

In the second, a malicious host M sends packets using IPH as its source address. If M is on the same switch, SAVI1 discards the packet and may probe the old port. H is still there and answers with a secured NUD advertisement, so the binding stays. If M is on another switch, SAVI2 sends a secured NUD solicitation and M cannot answer because it does not own the CGA, so the state returns to NO_BIND. In both cases the RFC notes that processing of further packets from M's port may be rate-limited to protect CPU.
sections.eli5: If a kid moves seats and says so, the old seat is checked and found empty, so the new seat is accepted. If a faker takes a seat, the real kid still answers the quiz and the faker cannot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SEND SAVI uses only validated SEND messages to create bindings, so packets from non-SEND nodes are discarded by the first SEND SAVI device and attackers gain nothing by skipping SEND. Nodes MUST NOT assume every SEND message coming from a SEND SAVI device was validated, since only the messages needed for SAVI are checked. The main requirement is that perimeter ports SHOULD be Validating. Otherwise an attacker can send packets from any source address.

Replay attacks. SEND alone limits replays only to a short time window, which is not enough for SAVI. SEND SAVI forwards DAD solicitations only to ports that previously held a binding for the address, and sends NUD advertisements only on the tested port, so an attacker must forge a valid DAD solicitation, which is deemed unfeasible.

Denial of service. When database memory runs out, the RFC RECOMMENDS replacing the entries with a higher creation time, so older entries survive. The RFC also RECOMMENDS reserving memory for at least four bindings per port. It MUST limit memory for stored data packets. Because cryptographic checks are costly, rate-limiting packets that trigger SEND SAVI events SHOULD be enforced per port.

Residual threat and privacy. If an attacker stops a host from defending its address, it can destroy the binding and create a new one. A device MUST delete binding anchor information as soon as the state returns to NO_BIND, unless it is likely to be involved in detecting, preventing or tracing spoofing.
sections.eli5: Copycats cannot easily fool the check, but they could try to tire out the guard with lots of fake requests. So the guard limits requests per door and forgets old notes quickly.
